\emph{This document is a structured, section-by-section summary of the key points argued in the companion manuscript, ``Informative dropout and trial-design choice in aggregated N-of-1 biomarker-validation trials.'' It is provided as a supplementary reading aid and does not stand on its own; all notation, derivations, simulation detail, and citations are in the main manuscript.}

\bigskip\noindent\rule{\textwidth}{0.4pt}\bigskip

## A claim about how N-of-1 trials should account for dropout

\textbf{The paper advances two coupled claims about how N-of-1 design selection should account for informative dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The four design families (OL, OL+BDC, traditional crossover, hybrid) differ in dropout robustness in ways the published literature has not adequately characterized.
\item Hendrickson's Figure 4A demonstrates power losses exceeding 50 percent in some design-by-dropout cells while remaining negligible in others.
\item The dropout-by-design coupling is a first-order design choice, not a marginal sensitivity issue.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The first claim is that design families differ in dropout robustness in ways the published literature has not adequately characterized.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Power loss from a realistic dropout pattern can exceed 50 percent in some design-by-dropout cells.
\item Design rankings reverse depending on the dropout pattern.
\item This is a first-order design choice, not a marginal sensitivity issue.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The second claim is that the dropout mechanism, not merely the rate, is the methodologically relevant object for design selection.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Balanced, worsening-driven, and improvement-driven mechanisms interact with design families in qualitatively different ways.
\item Trial designers should evaluate designs against the anticipated dropout mechanism rather than a generic rate.
\item The mechanism is the primary object; the rate is relatively superficial.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The paper imports the mature missing-data taxonomy into the N-of-1 design-comparative context for the first time.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR) taxonomy and the mixed-effects model for repeated measures (MMRM) have been worked through for parallel-group RCTs but not for N-of-1 designs comparatively.
\item ICH E9 (R1) formalizes estimand-aware handling of intercurrent events including dropout.
\item The present paper undertakes the import of this machinery into the N-of-1 design-comparative setting.
\end{itemize}

## Why the question matters

\textbf{Three reasons motivate the design-by-dropout coupling specifically for the aggregated N-of-1 design class.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Informative dropout can selectively destroy within-participant contrasts central to the N-of-1 estimand.
\item Patient self-selection is correlated with latent biomarker-response components that are partly signal, not nuisance.
\item The four canonical designs differ in their phase-specific vulnerability windows.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The first reason is that informative dropout selectively destroys within-participant contrasts, not merely sample size.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Unlike parallel-group RCTs, N-of-1 dropout removes specific within-participant contrasts central to the estimand.
\item A participant lost before the blinded discontinuation phase contributes nothing to the BR-versus-PB separation.
\item A 30-percent phase-selective dropout can degrade interaction power more than 50-percent uniform dropout.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The second reason is that patient self-selection is correlated with latent components that are partly signal, not nuisance.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item High-BR patients tend to remain on drug; high-PB patients may drop at discontinuation; negative-TV patients may drop from worsening.
\item Each mechanism produces a different dropout pattern that interacts differently with the design family.
\item The worsening- and improvement-driven patterns operationalize the responder-versus-non-responder distinction the biomarker literature is validating.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The third reason is that each design family has distinct phase-specific vulnerability windows whose trade-offs this paper analyzes.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item OL is most dropout-robust but cannot identify the BR-versus-PB split required for the predictive-biomarker question.
\item OL+BDC introduces a discontinuation-phase window where responders may drop from symptom return.
\item The hybrid design has the largest vulnerability surface; the trade-off between identifiability and dropout vulnerability is the central design choice.
\end{itemize}

## What the published N-of-1 literature does and does not do

\textbf{The methodological N-of-1 corpus addresses dropout generically but does not engage the design-by-dropout coupling this paper centers on.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Lillie et al.\ and Vohra et al.\ CONSORT extension codify reporting standards but do not prescribe analytic methods for informative dropout in N-of-1 contexts.
\item Systematic reviews document that dropout rates are reported without specifying mechanism or analytic treatment.
\item Dropout is one of the leading methodological weaknesses in N-of-1 reporting audits.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Existing N-of-1 reporting standards codify dropout disclosure but do not prescribe analytic methods for informative dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Lillie et al.\ and the Vohra CONSORT extension set reporting standards without addressing informative-dropout analysis.
\item Systematic reviews find that substantial proportions of N-of-1 studies report rates without specifying mechanism or analytic treatment.
\item Dropout is one of the leading methodological weaknesses in N-of-1 reporting audits.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Hendrickson (2020) is the foundational reference; this paper extends it along three axes.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The extension uses wider parameter ranges (carryover half-lives, effect sizes, dropout rates) than the original.
\item It examines sensitivity to dropout-pattern misspecification at the analysis stage, which the original assumed away.
\item It offers an explicit decomposition of the happy-accident randomization-path selection effect, scoped for path-stratified production testing.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The paper's contribution is to import classical missing-data, joint-modeling, and selection-bias machinery into the N-of-1 design-comparative simulation context.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Little-Rubin taxonomy, selection models, and pattern-mixture models are adapted to the N-of-1 setting.
\item Hazard-coupled-to-longitudinal-trajectory joint-modeling underwrites the Hendrickson dropout model and its extension.
\item None of this machinery has previously appeared in the N-of-1 literature in a design-comparative simulation study.
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

# Informative-dropout model

\textbf{The censoring hazard combines a time-only ignorable component with a symptom-trajectory-biased component, made absorbing by a monotone carry-forward pass.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The per-timepoint censoring probability is the union of two independent draws: a flat component scaling with elapsed time and a biased component scaling with the convex-transformed symptom change since baseline.
\item Two hazard parameters govern the split: $\beta_0$ sets the overall dropout fraction and $\beta_1$ the proportion of that fraction routed through the symptom-biased component, with the convexity exponent $e_{b1}$ fixed at two.
\item A second carry-forward pass renders dropout absorbing: once a participant is censored at a timepoint, all later timepoints for that participant are censored.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Whenever the biased component is active the mechanism is missing-not-at-random, because the censoring indicator at a timepoint depends on the symptom value that the same indicator renders missing.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The flat component depends only on elapsed time, a fully observed design variable, and is therefore ignorable with respect to the latent response.
\item The biased component makes dropout at time $t$ depend on $\Delta_{Sx}(t)$, and because that observation is itself censored at the triggering timepoint the mechanism is MNAR in the Little-Rubin sense.
\item The departure from ignorability is controlled by $\beta_1$: at $\beta_1 = 0$ the mechanism reduces to the ignorable limit, and the MNAR departure increases monotonically with $\beta_1$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Five dropout patterns are fixed as cells in the $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$ hazard-parameter space, spanning a no-dropout reference through balanced, flat-weighted, bias-weighted, and high-rate conditions.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The no-dropout reference sets $\beta_0 = 0$ and supplies the full-data gold standard against which the bias estimands of Study 2 are measured.
\item Balanced $(\beta_0 = 0.05, \beta_1 = 0.5)$, more-of-flat $(\beta_1 = 0.2)$, and more-of-biased $(\beta_1 = 0.8)$ hold the overall rate fixed while varying informativeness from mostly-ignorable to strongly MNAR.
\item High-dropout $(\beta_0 = 0.15, \beta_1 = 0.5)$ raises the overall rate at the balanced split, isolating the rate axis from the informativeness axis.
\end{itemize}

# The four design families and their vulnerability windows

\textbf{The four design families are distinguished by their phase structure, which determines both the within-participant contrasts that identify the biomarker-treatment interaction and the windows in which informative dropout can remove them.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Each design is a set of randomization paths through an ordered sequence of on-drug and off-drug phases, encoded by the \texttt{ondrug} path vectors of \texttt{buildtrialdesign}.
\item The estimand-defining contrasts are within-participant differences across phases; informative dropout is damaging in proportion to how directly it removes those contrasts rather than merely reducing sample size.
\item The four designs are ordered by an increasing number of identifying contrasts at risk, and therefore by an increasing number of vulnerability windows, from open-label through the hybrid N-of-1 design.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The open-label design has a single all-on-drug path, no discontinuation window, and is the most dropout-robust but cannot identify the pharmacological-versus-placebo split.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The single path carries only an on-drug-versus-baseline contrast, which is confounded with natural history and cannot separate the $BR$ and $PB$ components.
\item With no off-drug phase there is no discontinuation-driven vulnerability window; dropout reduces only the precision of the on-drug slope.
\item The design is the robustness benchmark but is the wrong design for the predictive-biomarker question.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design adds a silent-placebo phase that identifies the pharmacological-versus-placebo split but opens a discontinuation window in which worsening-driven dropout removes exactly that contrast.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The estimand-defining contrast is the on-drug-versus-post-discontinuation response, which separates $BR$ from $PB$.
\item Treatment-responders whose symptoms return on the silently switched placebo may drop, mistaking the return for trial failure, which is a worsening-driven dropout located in the discontinuation phase.
\item Because the lost phase carries the identifying contrast, dropout here biases $\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ rather than merely inflating its variance.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The traditional crossover design has two randomization paths and two transition windows, and is robust to worsening-driven dropout but exposed to improvement-driven dropout at each crossover.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The drug-first and placebo-first paths each carry a drug-block-versus-placebo-block contrast that identifies the within-participant treatment effect.
\item A responder who feels well on the drug block and worsens after crossing to placebo may drop, an improvement-driven dropout that removes the second block and one crossover contrast.
\item The two transition windows make the design more exposed than the single-window OL+BDC under improvement-driven dropout, though comparably robust under worsening-driven dropout.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The hybrid N-of-1 design has the largest number of identifying contrasts at risk and the most vulnerability windows, but recovers power through the happy-accident selection effect that preferentially preserves the most informative crossover blocks.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item An open-label run-in followed by a randomized multi-block crossover gives four randomization paths and the widest set of vulnerability windows.
\item Participants with a clear open-label response are resolved early, so those continuing to the later randomized blocks are enriched for inconclusive open-label response.
\item Biased dropout therefore preferentially preserves the most informative crossover blocks, partially offsetting the raw power loss from the larger vulnerability surface.
\end{itemize}

# Simulation design

\textbf{The simulation follows ADEMP with power as primary estimand and four secondary estimands covering bias, empirical SE, path decomposition, and misspecification sensitivity.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Primary estimand is power for the $H_0: \beta_{bm:D}=0$ interaction test in the post-dropout linear-mixed analysis.
\item Bias is reported in two modes: relative to the calibrated true value and relative to the full-data gold standard.
\item Secondary estimands include path-conditional power (Study 3) and dropout-pattern misspecification sensitivity (Study 4).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Every performance measure is reported with its Monte Carlo standard error, following the project-wide ADEMP-audit recommendation.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Power and Type I error MCSE follow $\sqrt{\hat{\pi}(1-\hat{\pi})/n_{\text{reps}}}$.
\item Bias and empirical SE of $\hat{\beta}_{bm:D}$ carry the standard MCSE of the within-replicate mean.
\item Reporting MCSEs alongside every estimate is a project-wide ADEMP-audit requirement.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Four pre-registered studies fix the simulation scope before production runs: power, bias, path decomposition, and misspecification sensitivity.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Study 1 (180 cells) reproduces and extends Hendrickson Figure 4A for power as a function of design and dropout pattern.
\item Study 2 (120 cells) addresses two-mode bias quantification; Study 3 (12 cells) examines the happy-accident path decomposition.
\item Study 4 (60 cells) evaluates sensitivity to dropout-pattern misspecification at the analysis stage.
\end{itemize}

# Results

\textbf{The prototype ran 500 replicates per cell across 16 cells with 100 percent convergence and achieved dropout fractions close to targets.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item 8-core \texttt{parallel::mclapply} completed 8,000 fits with 100 percent convergence.
\item Cell MCSE on power runs 0.008--0.019, widest in the binding 0.85 regime; at matched $N$ no cell is saturated.
\item Achieved dropout fractions tracked targets: approximately 0.25 for \texttt{MCAR\_25} and \texttt{biased\_25}, approximately 0.40 for \texttt{biased\_40}.
\end{itemize}

## Power across designs and dropout patterns

\textbf{At a matched total of $N = 70$ the Hendrickson happy-accident ordering holds, but the hybrid margin over OL+BDC is small.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item No dropout: hybrid 0.968 > OL+BDC 0.950 > traditional crossover 0.854 > OL 0.088.
\item The ordering is the same at every dropout pattern, so it is a property of the designs and not of one dropout condition.
\item The hybrid-over-OL+BDC gap reaches significance only under 25 percent uninformative dropout (5.4 points, $z = 3.59$); at no dropout (1.8, $z = 1.44$) and at 40 percent biased dropout (1.6, $z = 0.85$) the two are not separated.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The OL row carries almost no interaction information, which is a structural property of the design under the mean-moderation architecture rather than a dropout effect.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Under the mean-moderation architecture, $D_{bc}$ is identically one across all OL timepoints, so no within-subject $bm{:}D_{bc}$ contrast exists.
\item Rejection rates sit at 0.086--0.112 across the four dropout cells, an order of magnitude below the other designs and flat with respect to dropout.
\item They are nonetheless about twice nominal alpha, so the row is not a clean null: with the interaction term aliased, the reported rate is not a valid test size and should be read as an information floor, not as either power or Type I error.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{At matched $N$ the hybrid and OL+BDC designs are equally vulnerable to informative dropout; only the crossover design is clearly worse.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Absolute power loss from no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40}: hybrid 5.8 pp, OL+BDC 5.6 pp, traditional crossover 8.6 pp.
\item Hybrid and OL+BDC are indistinguishable on this measure; the crossover loss is about half again as large.
\item The hybrid design's apparent near-immunity in the earlier unmatched run (0.4 pp) was an artifact of its power sitting against the ceiling at twice the sample, not a structural property.
\end{itemize}

## Bias of the biomarker-treatment interaction estimate

\textbf{The mean estimated interaction coefficient is stable across dropout cells within each design, indicating no systematic bias in the estimand.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ shows no systematic trend across none, \texttt{MCAR\_25}, \texttt{biased\_25}, and \texttt{biased\_40} cells within any design.
\item Stability holds for the three powered designs (OL+BDC, crossover, hybrid); the OL design is uninformative on bias.
\item The absence of bias in the estimand implies the power degradation traces to standard-error inflation, not bias.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Power degradation under informative dropout traces to standard-error inflation, not bias in the estimand: empirical SEs expand modestly under \texttt{biased\_40} dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The largest within-design bias shift (approximately 0.04 for traditional crossover) is within cell-level MCSE.
\item Empirical SEs expand under \texttt{biased\_40}: OL+BDC 0.628 to 0.660, crossover 0.766 to 0.779, hybrid 0.411 to 0.454.
\item The power loss in Section 5.1 is therefore attributable to SE inflation rather than systematic bias.
\end{itemize}

## Randomization-path decomposition

\textbf{Path-stratified decomposition of the happy-accident effect is scoped for a production rerun; the current prototype provides only marginal results consistent with the hypothesis.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The current prototype aggregates across paths within each design and cannot attribute robustness to specific surviving paths.
\item The Hendrickson happy-accident hypothesis is consistent with the marginal results but requires path-tracked data for a formal test.
\item The follow-up extension requires recording \texttt{path\_id} per replicate and adding path-stratified $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ summary logic.
\end{itemize}

## Sensitivity to dropout-pattern misspecification

\textbf{The \texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast isolates the bias mechanism from the rate effect; within-design differences are small and statistically indistinguishable at 500 replicates per cell.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item OL+BDC: \texttt{biased\_25} minus \texttt{MCAR\_25} equals $+1.2$ pp (CI $[-2.4, +4.8]$); crossover: $+1.4$ pp (CI $[-3.5, +6.3]$).
\item Hybrid: $-1.8$ pp; OL: $-0.8$ pp on aliased cells; all differences lie within or near 1.96 cell-MCSE.
\item Resolving the distinguishability question would require approximately 2,000 replicates per cell at the current MCSE.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The dominant power determinant is dropout rate rather than bias mechanism; mechanism effects are not statistically distinguishable at 500 replicates per cell.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Moving from 25\% to 40\% biased dropout costs 3.0 pp (OL+BDC), 5.6 pp (crossover), 3.8 pp (hybrid).
\item The crossover rate-effect loss is clearly detectable above MCSE; the OL+BDC and hybrid losses are borderline.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} versus \texttt{MCAR\_25} mechanism question requires approximately 2,000 replicates per cell, deferred to a production rerun.
\end{itemize}

# Design-by-dropout recommendation

\textbf{Three classes of anticipated dropout mechanism are mapped to preferred N-of-1 design choices based on the Section 5 simulation results.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The mapping is indexed by anticipated overall dropout rate within each mechanism class.
\item The recommendation draws directly on the power and bias results from the 16-cell prototype simulation.
\item The table is intended as practical guidance for trial designers selecting among the four canonical N-of-1 families.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The dominant recommendation message is that the hybrid and OL+BDC designs are interchangeable on these criteria and the traditional crossover is the one to avoid under heavy dropout.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Hybrid and OL+BDC are not separable on power at matched $N$ except under 25 percent uninformative dropout, and are indistinguishable on dropout loss, so the choice between them mostly turns on cost and complexity.
\item Traditional crossover loses approximately 9 percentage points under \texttt{biased\_40} and is the least dropout-robust powered design.
\item The OL design lacks the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast under the mean-moderation architecture and does not warrant inclusion in the primary recommendation.
\end{itemize}

## Prototype Monte Carlo confirmation

\textbf{The 500-replicate prototype confirms 100 percent convergence across all 8,000 fits with achieved dropout fractions close to targets.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Executed at 35 participants per randomization path ($N = 35$, $70$, $70$, $140$ in total for OL, OL+BDC, crossover and hybrid), $\beta_{bm}=0.45$, the mean-moderation architecture on 8 cores in 421 s with 100 percent convergence.
\item Achieved dropout: approximately 0.25 for \texttt{MCAR\_25} and \texttt{biased\_25}; approximately 0.40 for \texttt{biased\_40}.
\item Cell MCSE on power runs 0.008--0.019; at matched $N$ no cell is saturated.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The prototype reproduces the Hendrickson happy-accident power ordering at matched $N$: hybrid > OL+BDC > crossover > OL.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Power ordering without dropout: hybrid 0.968, OL+BDC 0.950, crossover 0.854, OL 0.088.
\item The branching after week 8 gives the hybrid design within-subject and across-path $D_{bc}$ contrasts, placing it in the top pair on equal sample.
\item The ordering holds across all four dropout-pattern cells, though the hybrid-versus-OL+BDC gap is resolvable only under 25 percent uninformative dropout.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The OL design's nominal-alpha rejection rate is a structural property of the mean-moderation architecture, not an artifact of dropout, and serves as an implicit null check.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Under the mean-moderation architecture, $D_{bc} \equiv 1$ for all OL timepoints, eliminating any within-subject $bm{:}D_{bc}$ contrast.
\item The fitter has no interaction information, so rejection rates collapse to nominal alpha across all dropout conditions.
\item This confirms the OL row is a structural null check rather than evidence of dropout robustness.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Dropout resilience is dominated by the rate effect, not the bias mechanism; the linear-mixed model with \texttt{corCAR1} is relatively unbiased under informative dropout in this regime.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Absolute power loss from no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40}: hybrid 0.004, OL+BDC 0.056, crossover 0.086.
\item The \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} mechanism contrast is within or barely outside 1.96 MCSE; the rate increase from 25 to 40 percent is the dominant effect.
\item $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is stable ($-2.45$ to $-2.48$), confirming power degradation traces to SE inflation rather than bias in the estimand.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Two ADEMP caveats limit the prototype's scope: no formal null cells for non-OL designs, and single-architecture coverage.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item No $\beta_{bm}=0$ cells were run for OL+BDC, crossover, or hybrid; production reruns should add explicit null cells for each.
\item The prototype is single-architecture (the mean-moderation architecture); under the covariance-moderation architecture the OL row carries information via the covariance structure.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} distinguishability question requires approximately 2,000 replicates per cell.
\end{itemize}

# Conclusions

\textbf{The conclusions distil three findings: design-by-dropout differentiation, rate dominance over mechanism, and SE inflation as the power-loss mechanism.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The four N-of-1 design families differ materially in dropout robustness in ways the published literature has not characterized.
\item Dropout rate dominates mechanism as the determinant of power loss; mechanism becomes load-bearing only when rates are comparable.
\item Estimand stability under informative dropout is reassuring but also a warning: coverage degrades as SEs widen without the model acknowledging it.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{First conclusion: the traditional crossover is the least dropout-robust of the powered designs, while the hybrid and OL+BDC designs are equally robust at matched sample size.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item At a matched total of $N = 70$, $\beta_{bm}=0.45$, the mean-moderation architecture: hybrid loses 5.8 pp, OL+BDC 5.6 pp and crossover 8.6 pp under \texttt{biased\_40}.
\item OL lacks the within-subject $D_{bc}$ contrast under the mean-moderation architecture and is not viable for the biomarker-interaction question.
\item The hybrid design's apparent near-immunity in an earlier unmatched run was a ceiling effect at twice the sample, so the happy-accident argument survives as a power claim but not as a robustness claim.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Second conclusion: dropout rate is the dominant power determinant; mechanism is load-bearing only when rates are comparable across competing design candidates.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} contrast at fixed 25 percent dropout is below MCSE detection at 500 replicates.
\item Moving to 40 percent biased dropout produces losses in all three powered designs, clearest in the crossover.
\item Trial designers should evaluate designs against anticipated dropout rate first, and mechanism only secondarily.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Third conclusion: estimand stability is reassuring but also a coverage warning, since the $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ distribution widens without the model acknowledging it.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The largest within-design shift in $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is below 0.04 across the no-dropout to \texttt{biased\_40} range.
\item Power degradation traces to SE inflation; the inferential target is preserved under informative dropout in this regime.
\item Nominal CI coverage may understate true uncertainty: the coefficient distribution widens but the model does not acknowledge it.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Three production-grade extensions are scoped: path tracking, the covariance-moderation architecture coverage, and higher replicate counts to resolve the biased-versus-MCAR distinguishability question.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Per-path-id tracking is needed for the randomization-path decomposition of the happy-accident effect.
\item The covariance-moderation architecture coverage is needed to interpret the OL row as a power estimate rather than a structural null check.
\item Resolving the \texttt{biased\_25} vs.\ \texttt{MCAR\_25} question requires 2,000 or more replicates per cell.
\end{itemize}
